literal: Wei Cao, style name Deyuan, was a man of Dai.
idiomatic: Wei Cao, styled Deyuan, came from Dai.

literal: In youth he mastered chivalry and had talent and stratagem.
idiomatic: As a youth he excelled at chivalric ways and showed talent and strategic sense.

literal: Jin's General Who Pacifies the North Wei Guan took Cao as gate commander.
idiomatic: The Jin General Who Pacifies the North, Wei Guan, appointed Cao gate commander.

literal: In the time of Divine Yuan he often attached himself to the court.
idiomatic: During the reign of Emperor Shenyuan he cultivated close ties with the state.

literal: After Shenyuan's death, with his nephew Xiong and kinsmen and fellow-townsmen Ji Dan and others he came to submit, urging the Huan and Mu emperors to recruit Jin men.
idiomatic: After Shenyuan died, he came in with his nephew Xiong, kinsmen, and fellow-townsmen such as Ji Dan and urged the Huan and Mu emperors to enlist Jin subjects.

literal: Emperor Huan made him chief minister and entrusted him with state affairs.
idiomatic: Emperor Huan made him chief minister and gave him charge of state affairs.

literal: When the Liu and Shi disorders broke out, Emperor Huan aided the Jin house.
idiomatic: When turmoil engulfed the Liu and Shi regimes, Emperor Huan supported the Jin.

literal: Cao was gradually promoted to Right General and enfeoffed Marquis of Dingxiang.
idiomatic: Cao rose step by step to Right General and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dingxiang.

literal: In early Huangxing, Yan Province Aide Duan Rong of Yanmen unearthed this stele at Dahang; though the text is not elegant, the matter deserves record, so it is briefly appended to the biography.
idiomatic: Early in Huangxing, Duan Rong, aide of Yan Province from Yanmen, dug up this stele at Dahang; the prose is plain, but the matter is worth preserving, so it is summarized here.

literal: Cao died in the third year of Emperor Mu.
idiomatic: Cao died in the third year of Emperor Mu's reign.

literal: At first those kinsmen and fellow-townsmen who entered the state with Cao—Wei Qin, Marquis of Anle Pavilion; Wei Chong and Wei Qing, both Marquises of the Capital Pavilion; Wei Shen and Duan Fan, both Generals of Trust and Righteousness and Marquises of the Capital District; Wang Fa, General Who Establishes Martial Might and Marquis of the Capital Pavilion; Fan Ban, General Who Breaks the Foe and Marquis of Guangwu Pavilion; Jia Qing, General Who Establishes Martial Might and Marquis of Shangluo Pavilion; Jia Xun, Marquis of the Capital Pavilion; Li Yi, Marquis Within the Passes; Guo Ru, Marquis Within the Domains—all were enfeoffed and appointed by Emperor Huan.
idiomatic: The kinsmen and fellow-townsmen who had entered the state with Cao were enfeoffed by Emperor Huan: Wei Qin as Marquis of Anle Pavilion; Wei Chong and Wei Qing as Marquises of the Capital Pavilion; Wei Shen and Duan Fan as Generals of Trust and Righteousness and Marquises of the Capital District; Wang Fa as General Who Establishes Martial Might and Marquis of the Capital Pavilion; Fan Ban as General Who Breaks the Foe and Marquis of Guangwu Pavilion; Jia Qing as General Who Establishes Martial Might and Marquis of Shangluo Pavilion; Jia Xun as Marquis of the Capital Pavilion; Li Yi as Marquis Within the Passes; and Guo Ru as Marquis Within the Domains.

literal: In the turmoil of Liuxiu, most of those who survived followed Liu Kun's envoy Ren Zun south in flight.
idiomatic: During the crisis of Liuxiu, most survivors followed Liu Kun's envoy Ren Zun in flight to the south.

literal: The names of Wei Xiong, Ji Dan, Mo Han, and others all appear on the stele.
idiomatic: Wei Xiong, Ji Dan, Mo Han, and others are all named on the stele.

literal: Xiong, style name Shiyuan, and Dan, style name Shiya, were both bold and resourceful; both emperors Huan made them generals and they constantly followed campaigns.
idiomatic: Xiong, styled Shiyuan, and Dan, styled Shiya, were bold and full of schemes; both were made generals by Emperor Huan and regularly joined campaigns.

literal: Xiong was gradually promoted to Left General and Marquis of Yunzhong.
idiomatic: Xiong rose to Left General and Marquis of Yunzhong.

literal: Dan also became famous for martial deeds; late in Emperor Huan's reign he reached General of Trust and Righteousness and Marquis of Loufan.
idiomatic: Dan likewise won renown in battle; late in Emperor Huan's reign he became General of Trust and Righteousness and Marquis of Loufan.

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Mu both were entrusted with office; after Wei Cao's death they both served as left and right chief ministers.
idiomatic: At the start of Emperor Mu's reign both were heavily relied upon; after Wei Cao died they served together as chief ministers of the left and right.

literal: In Liuxiu's rebellion the realm fell into great disorder; Xiong and Dan were both embraced by popular sentiment, and with Liu Zun they led tens of thousands of Wuhuan and Jin men in revolt.
idiomatic: When Liuxiu rebelled and the realm convulsed, Xiong and Dan won popular support and, with Liu Zun, led tens of thousands of Wuhuan and Jin subjects in revolt.

literal: Liu Kun heard of it and was greatly pleased; he came to Pingcheng to comfort and accept them, intending thereby to destroy Shi Le.
idiomatic: Liu Kun was delighted, went to Pingcheng to welcome them, and hoped to use them to destroy Shi Le.

literal: Later they were destroyed by Le's general Kong Chang.
idiomatic: They were later destroyed by Kong Chang, a general of Shi Le.

literal: Mo Han was a man of Fanchi in Yanmen.
idiomatic: Mo Han came from Fanchi in Yanmen.

literal: When Liu Kun held Bing Province he recruited Han as an aide.
idiomatic: When Liu Kun governed Bing Province he took Han on as an aide.

literal: Han lived near the frontier and often had dealings within the state.
idiomatic: Han lived near the border and kept up regular contact with the court.

literal: Emperor Mu prized his talent and capacity.
idiomatic: Emperor Mu admired his ability.

literal: When he became King of Dai he fully staffed his officials and sought Han from Kun; Kun instructed Han to go.
idiomatic: When he became King of Dai he formed a full bureaucracy and asked Kun for Han; Kun urged Han to go.

literal: He then entered to take part in state office and constantly joined in great plans of state.
idiomatic: He entered government service and regularly took part in major state deliberations.

literal: He died holding Left General and Marquis Within the Passes.
idiomatic: He died as Left General and Marquis Within the Passes.

literal: His old residence lay south of the Sanggan River; the world calls it Mo Han's cliff—"Han" being a corrupted pronunciation—or sometimes Mo Hui City.
idiomatic: His old home stood south of the Sanggan; people call it Mo Han's Cliff—"Han" being a corrupted form of the name—or Mo Hui City.

literal: His son Xian, in the age of Zhaocheng, was Left Regular Attendant.
idiomatic: His son Xian served as Left Regular Attendant under Emperor Zhaocheng.

literal: Xian's son Ti, at the beginning of Daowu, was a great general and for merit was granted the title Marquis of Dongwan.
idiomatic: Xian's son Ti, in Emperor Daowu's early reign, became a great general and was enfeoffed Marquis of Dongwan for his achievements.

literal: He often attended banquets with Li Li; Li was punished for disrespect in seating, and Ti was also demoted to Governor of Jiyang.
idiomatic: He often shared banquets with Li Li; when Li was punished for irreverence at table, Ti was demoted to Governor of Jiyang.

literal: Later Daowu wished to enlarge the palaces and measured several tens of li around Pingcheng, intending to model Ye, Luoyang, and Chang'an, and transported several million timbers.
idiomatic: Later Emperor Daowu planned to expand the palace complex, surveyed tens of li around Pingcheng on the model of Ye, Luoyang, and Chang'an, and requisitioned millions of beams.

literal: Because Ti was ingenious in craft, he was summoned to supervise the work.
idiomatic: Ti's mechanical skill led to his appointment as overseer of construction.

literal: Summoned in to discuss the design of the works, after long attendance he grew quite negligent and was granted death.
idiomatic: Called in to discuss the building plans, he grew slack during long attendance at court and was put to death.

literal: Ti's younger brother Yun loved learning and was skilled at archery.
idiomatic: Ti's younger brother Yun loved study and excelled at archery.

literal: In Daowu's time he regularly managed the Selection Bureau and was granted Marquis of Ande.
idiomatic: Under Emperor Daowu he ran the Selection Bureau and was enfeoffed Marquis of Ande.

literal: He was transferred to Commandant of the Imperial Carriages and joined in state deliberations.
idiomatic: He became Commandant of the Imperial Carriages and took part in state counsel.

literal: When Taiwu conquered Helian Chang, an edict ordered Yun and the Prince of Changshan, Su, to remain and garrison Tongwan, and he was advanced to Duke of Anding.
idiomatic: When Emperor Taiwu took Helian Chang, Yun and Prince Su of Changshan were ordered to hold Tongwan; Yun was promoted to Duke of Anding.

literal: Yun comforted old and new alike, and all found their place.
idiomatic: Yun reassured old subjects and new, and all were settled.

literal: On his death he was posthumously titled Duke Jing.
idiomatic: After his death he received the posthumous title Duke Jing.

literal: Liu Kuren, style name Meigen, was of the Dugu tribe, a clansman of Liu Wu.
idiomatic: Liu Kuren, styled Meigen, belonged to the Dugu tribe and was kin to Liu Wu.

literal: In youth he was bold and chivalrous, with wisdom and stratagem.
idiomatic: In youth he was daring and chivalrous, with wit and strategy.

literal: His mother was a daughter of Emperor Pingwen.
idiomatic: His mother was a daughter of Emperor Pingwen.

literal: Emperor Zhaocheng again gave him a clanswoman in marriage and made him Grand Chieftain of the Southern Tribes.
idiomatic: Emperor Zhaocheng again married him to a clanswoman and appointed him Grand Chieftain of the Southern Tribes.

literal: In the thirty-ninth year of Jianguo Zhaocheng died suddenly; Daowu was not yet enthroned, and Fu Jian made Kuren General Who Crosses the River and Marquis Within the Passes.
idiomatic: In the thirty-ninth year of Jianguo, Zhaocheng died suddenly before Daowu had taken the throne; Fu Jian made Kuren General Who Crosses the River and Marquis Within the Passes.

literal: He ordered him and Wei Chen to divide the tribal masses and rule them—the west of the river to Chen, the east to Kuren.
idiomatic: He set Kuren and Wei Chen to divide the tribal following: the west of the river to Chen, the east to Kuren.

literal: Thereupon the Xianming Empress brought Daowu and the princes of Wei and Qin from the Helan tribe to dwell there.
idiomatic: The Xianming Empress then brought Daowu and the Wei and Qin princes from the Helan tribe to live under Kuren's protection.

literal: Kuren served with full loyalty and did not change his devotion with rise or fall.
idiomatic: Kuren served with steadfast loyalty, unmoved by fortune or ruin.

literal: Fu Jian placed Wei Chen beneath Kuren; Chen was enraged, rebelled, and attacked Kuren.
idiomatic: Fu Jian ranked Wei Chen below Kuren; Chen in anger rebelled and attacked him.

literal: Kuren attacked Chen and defeated him.
idiomatic: Kuren struck Chen and routed him.

literal: Fu Jian granted Kuren's wife the Lady Gongsun and enriched her dowry.
idiomatic: Fu Jian gave Kuren's wife the surname Gongsun and sent a lavish dowry.

literal: Murong Chui besieged Fu Pi at Ye and also sent a general, Ping Gui, to attack Fu Jian's Yan Province governor Wang Yong at Ji.
idiomatic: Murong Chui besieged Fu Pi at Ye and sent Ping Gui to attack Wang Yong, Fu Jian's governor of Yan Province, at Ji.

literal: Kuren sent his wife's elder brother Gongsun Xi to aid Yong in striking Gui and inflicted a great defeat.
idiomatic: Kuren sent his brother-in-law Gongsun Xi to help Yong against Gui and won a crushing victory.

literal: Kuren again was about to lead a major force to rescue Pi.
idiomatic: Kuren prepared to march in force to relieve Pi.

literal: He mobilized troops from Yanmen, Shanggu, and Dai commanderies and halted at Fanzhi.
idiomatic: He raised troops from Yanmen, Shanggu, and Dai and camped at Fanzhi.

literal: Earlier, Murong Wen and others, who were to be relocated to Chang'an, had fled to Kuren's tribe and constantly thought of returning east.
idiomatic: Earlier Murong Wen and others, slated for relocation to Chang'an, had taken refuge with Kuren and longed to go east again.

literal: In this campaign Wen and others by night led men of the three commanderies, attacked and killed Kuren, seized his swift horses, and fled to Murong Chui.
idiomatic: On this campaign Wen and others led men of the three commanderies by night, killed Kuren, took his best horses, and fled to Murong Chui.

literal: Gongsun Xi, hearing of the turmoil, fled to the Dingling.
idiomatic: Gongsun Xi, hearing of the upheaval, fled to the Dingling.

literal: Kuren's younger brother Juan succeeded to govern the tribe's affairs.
idiomatic: Kuren's younger brother Juan took charge of tribal affairs.

literal: Juan's third son Luo Chen, alert and wise in stratagem, said to Juan, "Cousin Xian is a cruel man—I wish you would plot against him early.
idiomatic: Juan's third son Luo Chen, sharp and full of schemes, told Juan, "Cousin Xian is ruthless; you should deal with him soon.

literal: " Juan paid no heed.
idiomatic: Juan paid no attention.

literal: Later Kuren's son Xian indeed killed Juan and replaced him.
idiomatic: Later Kuren's son Xian killed Juan and seized power.

literal: Once Xian had killed Juan he also plotted rebellion.
idiomatic: After killing Juan, Xian also plotted rebellion.

literal: When Daowu took the throne he attacked Xian at Mayi, pursued him to Mize, and inflicted a great defeat.
idiomatic: When Daowu came to the throne he attacked Xian at Mayi, pursued him to Mize, and routed him.

literal: Later he fled to Murong Lin; Lin moved him to Zhongshan.
idiomatic: He later fled to Murong Lin, who resettled him at Zhongshan.

literal: Luo Chen was also the elder brother of the Xuanmu Empress.
idiomatic: Luo Chen was the elder brother of the Xuanmu Empress.

literal: After Xian killed Juan, Luo Chen fled to Daowu.
idiomatic: When Xian killed Juan, Luo Chen fled to Daowu.

literal: Xian relied on his strength and often plotted rebellion; Luo Chen always reported it first.
idiomatic: Xian, trusting in his power, repeatedly plotted revolt; Luo Chen always warned the throne in advance.

literal: He was appointed Grand Chieftain of the Southern Tribes.
idiomatic: He was made Grand Chieftain of the Southern Tribes.

literal: Following the pacification of the Central Plains, for merit he was granted Duke of Yong'an.
idiomatic: After the conquest of the Central Plains he was enfeoffed Duke of Yong'an for his service.

literal: For military achievement he was made General Who Pacifies the East and Governor of Ding Province.
idiomatic: For military merit he became General Who Pacifies the East and Governor of Ding Province.

literal: On his death his posthumous title was Jing.
idiomatic: He died with the posthumous title Jing.

literal: His son Shuhui inherited the title, held the post of Governor of Bing Province, and died.
idiomatic: His son Shuhui inherited the title, served as Governor of Bing Province, and died.

literal: His son Qiuyin held the post of General of the Martial Guard.
idiomatic: His son Qiuyin was General of the Martial Guard.

literal: On his death his posthumous title was Zhen.
idiomatic: He died with the posthumous title Zhen.

literal: His son Ertou held the posts of magistrate of Weichang and Yingtao counties and was posthumously made Governor of Julu.
idiomatic: His son Ertou was magistrate of Weichang and Yingtao and was posthumously named Governor of Julu.

literal: His son Renzhi, style name Shanjing, in youth had moral resolve and had roughly browsed histories.
idiomatic: His son Renzhi, styled Shanjing, showed moral fiber in youth and had read history in a general way.

literal: He held the posts of General of the Guard and Governor of Western Yan Province and at his post won contemporary renown.
idiomatic: He served as General of the Guard and Governor of Western Yan Province and earned a reputation in his day.

literal: He died in the second year of Wuding and was posthumously made Grand General of the Guard, Minister of the Civil Service, and Governor of Qing Province, with posthumous title Jing.
idiomatic: He died in the second year of Wuding and was posthumously made Grand General of the Guard, Minister of the Civil Service, and Governor of Qing Province, with the posthumous title Jing.

literal: Outwardly Renzhi appeared a man of virtue; inwardly he was full of pretense.
idiomatic: Renzhi posed as a man of virtue while inwardly he was full of artifice.

literal: Toward guests he broke beds and worn mats, served coarse rice and cold dishes, and wore old, foul clothes—yet he overbore his subordinates.
idiomatic: With guests he used broken beds and threadbare mats, coarse rice and cold dishes, and shabby clothes—yet he bullied those beneath him.

literal: He was skilled at watching those in power and could perform crafty provocations.
idiomatic: He watched those in power keenly and knew how to stage theatrical outbursts.

literal: Often in dense crowds he would beat some corrupt official or release some lone poor man, declaiming loudly to dazzle others; shallow minds all praised his goodness.
idiomatic: In crowded gatherings he might thrash a corrupt clerk or spare a lone beggar, declaiming for effect; the shallow praised him as noble.

literal: His reputation for public ability far exceeded the fact.
idiomatic: His fame for public spirit far outran the reality.

literal: His nature was also cruel; at Jinyang he once undertook city-wall works, and Renzhi directed the labor.
idiomatic: He was also brutal; at Jinyang he once oversaw repairs to the city walls under Renzhi's supervision.

literal: For slight delay he beat the former Governor of Yin Province Pei Yuan and the Governor of Bing Province Wang Chuo.
idiomatic: For minor tardiness he had Pei Yuan, former governor of Yin Province, and Wang Chuo, governor of Bing Province, flogged.

literal: Qi Emperor Shenwu rebuked him severely.
idiomatic: Qi Emperor Shenwu censured him harshly.

literal: He loved written texts by nature.
idiomatic: He had a natural love of the written word.

literal: If clerical writing lost proper form he would add flogging;
idiomatic: Clerical errors in format earned a beating;

literal: if pronunciation was slightly off he also met the cudgel, and clerks suffered greatly for it.
idiomatic: even slight slips in tone brought the rod, and clerks suffered for it.

literal: Yet he loved literature and history and respected men of talent.
idiomatic: Yet he cherished literature and history and treated men of talent with respect.

literal: He was on intimate terms with the guard officer Feng Yuanxing.
idiomatic: He was close to the guard officer Feng Yuanxing.

literal: Years after Yuanxing's death Renzhi still looked after his household and often gave lavish aid; people esteemed him for this.
idiomatic: Years after Yuanxing died, Renzhi still tended his family with generous support, and contemporaries admired him for it.

literal: Renzhi's elder uncle Qi Gui, in the Zhenjun era, was made Palace Attendant.
idiomatic: Renzhi's elder uncle Qi Gui was appointed Palace Attendant in the Zhenjun era.
